brand.title: ESourceAIG (Production)
brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — J. F. Pennebaker Employee Benefits and Handbook

questions.question: Who is the primary HR contact at J. F. Pennebaker Co. for policy questions and concerns?
choices: Your direct supervisor
Melissa Massey
The company CEO
Any member of management
questions.feedback_correct: That's right—Melissa Massey is your first point of contact for any policy question, concern, or accommodation request.
questions.feedback_incorrect: While supervisors and other managers are available, Melissa Massey is specifically identified as the primary HR contact you should reach out to first.

questions.question: What does "at-will employment" mean at J. F. Pennebaker Co.?
choices: The company must provide a reason before terminating an employee
Either you or the company can end the employment relationship at any time, for any reason or no reason, with or without notice
You are guaranteed employment for at least one year
An employee can only be fired for violating a handbook policy
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—at-will employment goes both ways, and neither party needs cause or advance notice to end the relationship.
questions.feedback_incorrect: At-will employment means either party can end the relationship at any time for any reason or no reason at all. No advance notice or cause is required.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a protected category under J. F. Pennebaker Co.'s equal opportunity policy?
choices: Military or veteran status
Sexual orientation
Marital status
Disability
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—while the company protects many categories, marital status is not listed among the protected categories in the handbook.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The company's protected categories include race, color, religion, national origin, sex (including sexual orientation and gender identity), age 40+, disability, genetic information, military/veteran status, and other statuses protected by law. Marital status is not among them.

questions.question: What is the key difference between quid pro quo harassment and hostile work environment harassment?
choices: Quid pro quo harassment is only illegal if it results in termination, while hostile work environment is always illegal

Quid pro quo involves an exchange of a benefit or threat for sexual attention, while hostile work environment is unwelcome conduct based on a protected class that is severe or pervasive enough to interfere with work
Hostile work environment can only come from a supervisor, while quid pro quo can come from anyone
Quid pro quo harassment must be reported immediately, while hostile work environment can be reported later
questions.feedback_correct: You've got it—quid pro quo is about an exchange (something for something), while hostile work environment is about unwelcome conduct based on a protected class that is severe or pervasive.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Quid pro quo harassment specifically involves offering a benefit or making a threat in exchange for sexual attention. Hostile work environment is different—it's about unwelcome conduct based on a protected class that is severe or pervasive enough to interfere with work.

questions.question: What is your protection status if you participate in an investigation into someone else's discrimination complaint?
choices: You are not protected because you were not the person harassed
You are only protected if the investigation finds that a violation occurred
You are protected regardless of whether the investigation finds a violation
You have no protection unless you file your own complaint
questions.feedback_correct: Absolutely—participating in an investigation is protected conduct, and that protection applies regardless of the investigation's outcome.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Participating in an investigation is protected by company policy whether or not a violation is found. The company's protection covers the act of participation itself, not just the result.

questions.question: Based on the employment classifications described, which classification would give you company benefits but NOT eligibility for overtime pay?
choices: Full-Time Non-Exempt
Part-Time Non-Exempt
Temporary
Exempt
questions.feedback_correct: Right—Exempt employees receive company benefits but are not eligible for overtime pay. Full-Time Non-Exempt gets both benefits and overtime; Part-Time Non-Exempt gets overtime but not benefits; Temporary gets neither.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Review the four classifications: Full-Time Non-Exempt gets overtime and benefits, Part-Time Non-Exempt gets overtime but not benefits, Temporary gets neither, and Exempt gets benefits but not overtime.

questions.question: You believe your supervisor has violated a company policy, but you're unsure if it's serious enough to file a formal complaint. What should you do?
choices: Wait and see if the behavior happens again before reporting
Discuss it only with coworkers first to get their opinion
Reach out to Melissa Massey to talk through it, even if you're unsure
Report it to a different supervisor without contacting HR first
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—Melissa Massey welcomes conversations about uncertain situations. You can reach out just to talk through it without necessarily filing a formal complaint.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The course notes specifically state that if you're unsure whether something rises to the level of a formal complaint, you can reach out to Melissa Massey just to talk through it. She's the right person to call.

questions.question: Your company handbook states that all employees must keep company matters confidential. Can this policy legally prevent you from discussing wages with coworkers?
choices: Yes, because confidentiality policies override all other rights
Yes, but only if you sign an agreement acknowledging the policy
No, because Section 7 of the National Labor Relations Act protects your right to discuss wages, hours, and working conditions
No, but only if you are a union member
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—Section 7 NLRA rights cannot be taken away by any company policy, and no nondisclosure agreement can legally restrict them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Section 7 of the National Labor Relations Act gives every employee the right to discuss wages, hours, and working conditions with coworkers. No company policy, handbook, or nondisclosure agreement can legally remove or limit these rights.

questions.question: You report a concern about workplace safety to your supervisor, and shortly after, you notice you're being assigned worse shifts and excluded from team meetings. What should you do, and why?
choices: Accept the new assignments because you are at-will and the company can change your conditions anytime
Report the situation immediately to Melissa Massey as potential retaliation, because reporting concerns is protected conduct
Wait to see if the pattern continues before taking action
File a complaint with another supervisor instead of HR
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—reporting a concern is protected conduct, and retaliation for that report is prohibited. You should contact Melissa Massey right away.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Reporting a concern is protected conduct, and the company will not tolerate retaliation from anyone. Changes in your schedule or team participation following your report could constitute retaliation and should be reported to Melissa Massey immediately.
